You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

import json
def f(g):
    H,W=len(g),len(g[0])
    o=[row[:] for row in g]
    seen=set(); comps=[]
    for r in range(H):
        for c in range(W):
            if g[r][c] and (r,c) not in seen:
                v=g[r][c]; st=[(r,c)]; comp=set()
                while st:
                    y,x=st.pop()
                    if (y,x) in seen: continue
                    seen.add((y,x)); comp.add((y,x))
                    for dy,dx in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
                        ny,nx=y+dy,x+dx
                        if 0<=ny<H and 0<=nx<W and g[ny][nx]==v and (ny,nx) not in seen: st.append((ny,nx))
                comps.append((v,sorted(comp)))
    # group fragments by (row,color) -> one bar per (row,color)
    groups={}
    for v,comp in comps:
        for r,c in comp: groups.setdefault((r,v),set()).add(c)
    shapes=[]
    for (br,v),cells in groups.items():
        csR=sorted(cells); mn, mx = csR[0], csR[-1]
        gaps=[c for c in range(mn,mx+1) if (br,c) not in cells]
        if len(gaps)>1: continue   # require single gap column
        c=gaps[0]
        # both horizontal neighbors of gap must be nonzero in input
        L=gsR=[None]
        nbz = (c>0 and g[br][c-1]!=0) and (c<W-1 and g[br][c+1]!=0)
        if not nbz: continue
        shapes.append((br,v,c,cells))
    shapes.sort(key=lambda s:s[0])
    colends=defaultdict(int)   # last fill row per gap column (-1 init)
    for br,v,c,cells in shapes:
        lo = colends[c]+1
        lo = max(lo,1)
        hi = br
        for rr in range(lo,hi+1):
            if o[rr][c]==0: o[rr][c]=v
        colends[c]=hi
    return o

                cnt={}

steps.text:
Now I have clear empirical data. Let me figure out the rule.

Demo 1:
- col3 (gap of color 2, bar row 9): filled rows 0-9 with color 2 — extends UP from bar to top edge, AND fills its own gap cell (row 9). So extension: up toward top edge, starting at bar row? It fills rows 0..9 = full column from top. Interesting: it goes to top edge including bar row itself (which had the gap... wait, input (9,3) was 0 and output has 2 there — yes fill gap cell too). Actually "extended_cells" for color 2 showed added only at col 3. Input bar 2 at cols 0-2 and 4-7 on row 9, gap at col 3. Fill upward from bar row to top edge.
- col9 (gap of color 3? no, wait): color 3 components at row 9 cols 8-8 and 10-14 → gap at col 9. Filled rows 0-9 with 3. Then below that, rows 10 with color 4. Color 4's component is vertical at col 9 rows 12-14; its gap? No, col 9 is a single cell wide for color 4 — the gap detection failed there. But in output, col 9 rows 10,11 are 4 — extending UP from color 4's bottom (row 14) ... wait rows 10,11, and 12-14 already 4. So color 4 extended upward through rows 10-13? Input col 9 has 4 at rows 12-14. Output col 9 rows 10-14 all 4. So it extends up until barrow? Bar for color 4 is ambiguous (single-column shape). It fills from just below... to the top of where? Row 10 to 14, stopping above the 3-filled column? The 3 filled col 9 up to row 9. So 4 fills from row 10 down to bottom (its own shape). Hmm but also stops at bottom edge. So rule: extend each shape vertically in BOTH directions? No—color 2 went up only.

Let's think differently: maybe each shape extends TOWARD the nearest edge? Or extends away from nearest other shape? Alternative: each line extends both ways until blocked by another line or edge. Check demo 2:
- col3: color 3 fills rows 0-3 (up from bar row 3 to top). color 4 fills rows 4-8 (down from bar row 8 to... row 8 is bar? bar row for color 4 is 8, fills 4-8?? That includes row 8 which is 4 in input already). Wait output col3 rows 4-8 are 4, and input col3 has 4 at row 8. So it extends UP from bar row 8 to row 4? And stops just before color 3's fill (row 3). Hmm color 3 fills 0-3, color 4 fills 4-8. Together they cover 0-8 continuously! Like stacking segments in a column: color 3 occupies rows 0-3, color 4 occupies rows 4-8. Both start at bar row and go to the other shape... Actually color 3 bar at row 3 extends DOWN? No—it fills rows 0-3, i.e., from top edge down to bar row. Color 4 bar at row 8 fills rows 4-8 = from bar row up? Or from some lower point?

New idea: each colored segment (bar with gap) gets a vertical line drawn through the gap column spanning between this segment and the NEXT segment of a different color along that column? Check: col3 in demo2: 3-segment at row 3, 4-segment at row 8, 1-segment at rows 11-14 (vertical line). Output: 3 fills 0-3, 4 fills 4-8, 1 fills 9-14? Actually 1 fills rows 9-14 at col 3. Yes! So each colored line spans the region between adjacent colored lines, filling from one shape's row to the next. In fact every changed column is fully covered: col3 fully covered rows 0-14, col9 fully covered rows 0-14 in demo2? Col9: color6 fills 0-6, color7 fills 7-8, and input has 5 at col9 rows 9-14 which stays 5. So col9 completely covered 0-14 as well (6:0-6, 7:7-8, 5:9-14). 

So the rule might be: each column containing any colored cells gets filled entirely? Demo 1 col0: output rows 10-14 are 2 — but input had 2 only at row 9 cols 0-2. Col0 output = 2 at rows 10-14 plus gap fill at row 9. So column 0 filled 10-14 with color 2 (the nearest shape above? there's no shape above in col0 except the bar at row 9). Hmm, so columns without gaps also get extended? 

Wait, recheck: demo1 changes in col 0 were listed under "to-color 2" only at (0,3)... no, col 0 changes: earlier printout "to-color 2 [(0,3),...]" was grouped by target color but entries were (r,c,a). All those were c=3. So col0 wasn't mentioned—meaning col0 had NO changes? But output row 10-14 col 0 shows '2'? Earlier printed demo1 output row10 "000300000400000" — col0 is '0'. Right! Row 10 col0=0. So columns aren't fully covered.

OK here's a cleaner hypothesis based on contiguous vertical runs per output column:

- Each color's shape is a horizontal bar with exactly one gap (or single cell).
- Through the gap column, a vertical line of that color is drawn.
- Direction and extent: it extends from the gap row toward the nearer... let's tabulate precisely:

Gap col assignments per demo:
D1: 2-shape bar row9 gaps {3} → fill col3 rows 0-9 (UP to top edge). 3-shape: bars at row9 (cols 8, 10-14) gap col 9 → fill rows 0-9 (also up to top!). 4-shape: vertical col9 rows 12-14 (no gap detected as bar) → fill col9 rows 10-14?? Wait that doesn't fit. Hmm, 4's shape is a vertical stub, not a bar. Its "gap"? Maybe treat vertical shapes symmetrically: the shape occupies rows 12-14 in col 9; extending upward from its top (row12) to row 10? Or from its center? Center row 13, up to 10? Down to 14.

Alternative interpretation: fill the entire gap COLUMN with that color, from the shape's bar row to the nearest OTHER shape in that column? D1 col9: 3-shape's gap at row9; next shape down in col9 is 4 at row12. So fill col9 rows 10-11 with 4? But actual fills: 3 fills 0-9, 4 fills 10-14? No wait—recheck: col9 output: rows0-9 = 3, row10=4, row11=4, rows12-14=4. Input col9: row9=0 (gap), rows10-14=0. So 4 filled rows 10-11 only (extending up from its shape at row12 to meet the 3-filled column). And 3 filled 0-9: from top edge to its gap row. Hmm, why does 3 go to top edge while 4 stops at row 10 (just below 3)?

Maybe: each shape extends toward the NEAREST other shape along that column; if none, extend to grid edge. For 3 (gap row 9): nearest shape below in col9 is 4 at row12 → fill rows 10-11 with... 4? But rows 10-11 are 4, not 3. Contradiction unless 3 fills upward and 4 fills downward? 3 fills 0-9 (upward from gap to top edge). 4 fills 10-14 (downward/continues its shape to bottom edge). 

D2 col3: 3 shape bar row3, gap col3 → fill 0-3 (up to top). 4 shape bar row8 gap col3 → fill 4-8?? That's from row 4 up to 8 — i.e., up to the 3-fill bottom+1. Not to top. Hmm. Unless the rule: fill from shape's row to the nearest other shape in that column (exclusive), using that shape's color?! Col3: nearest below 3-shape to 4-shape: 3-shape fills rows 0-3 (from its row up to top); 4-shape fills rows 4-8 (from its row up to the 3-shape's fill?). Circular.

Try yet another framing: the vertical fill connects each shape to the shape ABOVE it (or the grid edge if none above). Order shapes by row within a column:
- D1 col9: shapes: 3 at row9 (bar), 4 at row12. 3 fills 0-9 (to top edge, since nothing above). 4 fills 10-14?? If connecting to shape above: 4 would fill 10-11 to connect to 3. But it filled 10-14 = down to bottom.

Hmm what about: shape extends toward the FAR side? 3 fills from top edge to its bar (covering itself). 4 fills from its bar to bottom edge. I.e., each shape extends to the nearest EDGE in the direction AWAY from everything? 3: nearest edge above is top; 4: nearest edge below is bottom. Both "extend away from the rest". Check D2 col3: 3 fills 0-3 (top edge), 4 fills 4-8... why not to bottom? Because 1 fills 9-14. Shapes stacked: 3 (top), 4, 1 (bottom). Each fills between itself and the next shape in order? 3 fills 0-3: between top edge and itself? That means 3 extends upward FROM its bar to the edge. 4 fills 4-8: between 3's fill bottom (row3) and itself? No—4 fills 4-8 INCLUDING its own row, extending UPWARD. 1 fills 9-14: extending DOWNWARD from itself to bottom.

Pattern: shapes sort by row; consecutive pairs get connected: pair (3@row3, 4@row8) → fill gap rows 4-7 with... who? 4 filled them, 3 didn't. Pair (4@8, 1@11) → gap rows 9-10 filled by 1.

Alternative: each shape extends toward the NEAREST other shape, filling with ITS OWN color? 4→nearest below is 1 (row11) → fill rows 9-10 with 4? Actual: 1 filled 9-10. No.

Try: each shape fills the gap between itself and the next shape below with its own color, then the whole thing becomes contiguous? D2 col3: 3 fills 0-3 (up to edge?), 4 fills 4-8, 1 fills 9-14. As contiguous run, each shape owns the segment from previous shape's bottom+1 to its own top? For 3: no shape above, so own segment is 0-3 (its own rows). For 4: segment above 3's bottom: rows 4-8. For 1: segment below 4's bottom: rows 9-14.

D1 col9: shapes by row: 3 at row9, 4 at rows12-14. 3 owns 0-9? Under "segment from top edge to its top": 3's segment = rows 0-9 (since nothing above). 4's segment: rows 10-14. Contiguous! ✓
D3 col9: shapes: 7@2, 6@5, 5@11, and 1@14 (col1 though). Col9: 7 fills 0-2, 6 fills 3-5, 5 fills 6-11, 1 fills 12-13 (col1, separate). Contiguous from top! 
D3 col1: shapes: 8@3, 3@8, 9@11, 1@14. Fills: 8:0-3, 3:4-8, 9:9-11, 1:12-14. Contiguous ✓!!
D2 col3: 3:0-3, 4:4-8, 1:9-14. Contiguous ✓.
D1 col3: 2-shape bar row9 gap col3; fills 0-9 (from top to its bar), and nothing below (no other shape in col3). ✓ Contiguous from top.

So the rule: group colored cells into horizontal bars (with gaps); for each column, sort the shapes by their bar row; fill the entire column contiguously, assigning each segment... which color gets which segment? In col3 D1, only 2 present → all 2. When two shapes share a column, upper shape gets rows from top edge to its own row, lower shape gets from below-upper-to-bottom? But in D2 col3, 4 got rows 4-8 and 1 got 9-14. Uppermost gets top segment, each subsequent gets the segment between previous shape and itself? What about D3 col1: 8(0-3), 3(4-8), 9(9-11), 1(12-14) — each gets from prev_bottom+1 to its own bottom? 8: 0-3 (own rows + top). 3: 4-8 (own row 8 + above). 9: 9-11 (own rows 9-11). 1: 12-14 (own row 14 + above). Consistent with: each shape extends from just below the shape above it up to... its own bottom? Or up to the gap fill? Actually simpler: each shape fills from the row below the previous shape's bottom to its own bottom row (inclusive), where the first shape extends from top edge to its bottom.

Equivalently: scan columns; sorted shapes by bar row; accumulate: current_fill_row starts at -1 (top edge); for each shape in order: fill rows max(curr+1, ?)... In D3 col1, 9's shape spans rows 9-11 (vertical stub!) — its own cells already occupy 9-11. And it filled 9-11 exactly its own cells? Input col1: 9 at rows 9-11. Output same. So no new fill there. Shape 3@8 filled 4-8: its own cell at 8 plus rows 4-7 above. Shape 8@3 filled 0-3: own cell 3 + rows 0-2 above. Shape 1@14 filled 12-14? Own cell at 14 + rows 12-13 above? But input had 0 there; output rows 12,13 col1 = 1. Yes! So each shape extends UPWARD from just below the shape above it to its own row... but wait, 4 in D2 filled 4-8 upward, and 1 filled 9-14 upward too. What about downward extension? Nothing fills below the bottom-most shape. And within a shape, does it extend below its own row? In D1 col9, 4 filled 10-11 ABOVE it, not below. D3 col1, 9 filled nothing below (edge). 

But wait — do shapes always extend UP only? D1: 2-shape gap fill rows 0-9 (up). 3-shape gap fill rows 0-9 (up). D2: all up. D3: all up. But what if multiple shapes in a column and middle ones? D2 col9: 6@0-6, 7@7-8, 5@9-14. 6 fills 0-6 (its own + top). 7 fills 7-8 (own). 5 fills 9-14 (own + bottom!). 5 extended DOWNWARD to bottom edge. And 7 didn't extend up or down beyond itself. Hmm, so bottom-most extends down? D1 col9: bottom-most is 4 (rows12-14), filled 10-14 — extended UP to connect to 3. Doesn't extend down (already at bottom edge). D2 col3: bottom-most 1 filled 9-14 = down to edge. D3 col1: bottom-most 1 filled 12-14 = down to edge. D3 col9: bottom-most 5 filled 6-11 = down? Its own cells at 11 only... wait 5's component is at row 11 cols 6-8 & 10-14, gap col 9. Its own cells include col9? No. It filled 6-11 in col9: from below 6's bottom (row5) to its own row 11. That's an UPWARD extension filling the gap between 6 and itself. And 5 is bottom-most in col9; it didn't extend to bottom edge (rows 12-14 stay 0). Hmm! So bottom-most extends down in D2/D3 col1/col3 but NOT in col9.

Difference: in col9, is there another shape nearby? The 1-shape is at col1. Hmm. Maybe rule: connect CONSECUTIVE SHAPES in a column by filling the gap between them with... which color? D2 col3 gap rows 4-7 filled with 4 (lower shape's color). D2 col9 gap rows 7 filled with 7 (lower). D1 col9 gap 10-11 filled with 4 (lower). D3 col1 gaps 4-7, 9-10 filled by lower (3, 9). Then verify: D3 col1 gaps 4-7 (between 8@3 and 3@8) filled with 3 ✓; 9-10 filled with 9 ✓; 12-13 filled with 1 ✓. D1 col3: gap between 2's bar (row9) and nothing below → not filled by rule? But rows 0-8 filled with 2! Hmm.

Unless: shapes also fill from TOP edge down to themselves when there's no shape above. I.e.: for each shape in a column, filled range = [below_prev_shape_or_top, shape's own bottom]. Check: D1 col3: only 2-shape → 0-9 ✓ (own row 9 + from top). D1 col9: 3@9, 4@12-14 → 3: 0-9 ✓; 4: 10-14 ✓ (own rows 12-14, above it 10-11 filled by rule "gap between consecutive").     out=[r[:] for r in res]

        nz=[r for r in range(H) if out[r][c]!=0]
        for r in range(H):
            if out[r][c]!=0: continue
            up=[s for s in nz if s<r]; dn=[s for s in nz if s>r]
